- State API: `decision.record` (owner only; the direct channel is forced, so no caller can claim a chat turn), `decision.resolve-dispute`, `decision.ask`, `decision.dismiss-question`, `decision.link`, `decision.revalidate`, `decision.close-follow-up` and the queries `decision.get`, `.history`, `.authoritative`, `.context`, `.reliance`, `.propagation`, each with the service's own rights.
- `start.ts` builds a `DecisionService` for the API with the event and effect services. The dispatcher keeps its own instance (with generation); correctness lives in stored records and the stored guard, so the two agree.
- Composed test proves: non-owner refused; hypothetical words record nothing; repeat is not a new decision; a correction supersedes and the old stays visible marked; a stale session's conflicting word is surfaced, not applied; an implementation-hold gate blocks at the stored guard.
- Not done here (card C08b): recording from a chat turn (the chat interpreter's decision intent, which needs the turn's wording check), interrupting a running generation from the API's instance, and a composed run of link/propagate/revalidate across a paused and a restarted agent.

## M01 notes (meetings in the state API)

- State API: `meeting.schedule`, `meeting.update-schedule`, `meeting.call-urgent`, `meeting.settle` (commands) and `meeting.schedule-get`, `meeting.occurrence`, `meeting.planned` (queries), with `MeetingService`'s own rights (`meeting.manage` to schedule or call, project agenda rights for the rest). `start.ts` builds the service with `inquiries` and the pause service's availability. A schedule must name its `timeZone` here: the owner's `meeting.timeZone` setting is not wired into the API instance (card M01c); the dispatcher's instance runs the clock and invitations.
- Composed test (the schedule starts the day after the real clock, so the slot is unambiguous; the dispatcher's clock is simulated): a schedule through the API is created once per command ID; an agent without `meeting.manage` is refused; nothing exists before the slot; ticking at the slot creates one on-time occurrence however often the dispatcher ticks; after a restart two days on one catch-up occurrence (mode `catch-up`, `skippedCount` at least 1, a new ID) stands for the missed slots; a second restart at the same moment creates nothing more. An urgent call is accepted and readable.
- Not in the composed test, so M01 is partly proven: absent and paused participants withheld without a wake through the composed API with real agent records (proven in `meetings.test.ts`), agenda retained across occurrences, delivery of invitations (no host sink composed). These are cards M01b (participants, agenda through the API) and M01c (the owner's `meeting.timeZone` setting in the API instance, and the invitation sink).
## H02 notes (remote workers composed into the controller)

- New `RemoteWorkerHost` (production `WorkerHost` over `RemoteWorkerService.place`; the operator supplies what an attempt needs of the host (`requirements`, never a default policy) and its inputs). `dispatch.remote` in `startController` takes `blobDirectory` (the controller's own artifact folder), optional transport settings (loopback by default; beyond it `allowRemote`, TLS and `publicHosts`), the protocol range and the hosts. The composer builds the artifact and remote services, adds the hosts after the local ones, binds the dispatcher's `storeOwner` to `RemoteWorkerService.storeOwner`, listens, and closes the listener with the workers. `DispatchHandle.workerUrl` says where workers connect.
- Review fixes: a handle acts only under its own placement number (after a move an old handle controls nothing); the checkpoint wait compares the placement's sequence instead of reading the blob each poll and defaults to 5 seconds (shutdown waits that long per remote attempt); a failed listen closes the local worker host.
- Composed test (proves only composed placement and protocol negotiation): an incompatible protocol is refused at connect; a compatible worker connects, is offered the attempt placed by the dispatcher's tick, receives the controller's own order, and its host credential is refused (`forbidden`) when it tries to create a project; `hostOfAgent` names the remote host.
- (The `requirements` refusal is now proven; the rest stands.) Unproven in the composed controller (card H02b): partition and delayed-packet fencing, an unsupported host failing visibly (`requirements` refusal), no self-promotion, relocation with integrity and policy refusals, the exclusive native-store owner, result/stop/checkpoint paths through the production host, and failure paths after a successful listen (driver or MCP construction) closing the listener. These are proven in `remote/*.test.ts` with a test host class against the same services.
- Not composed: the operator-facing configuration of hosts and their requirements from a settings file (the options are code-level here), and the exclusive-store-owner check across two live remote hosts in the composed controller.
- Known limits recorded for card H02b (second review): the placement check in the handle is check-then-act (`control()` takes no placement number, so a move committing between the check and the control call lands the old handle's message in the new placement); the checkpoint wait does not re-check the placement and a new host's checkpoint can satisfy an old handle's wait (the sequence carries over a move); a failure of `FileBlobStore.open` or remote-service construction after the local host was built still leaves that host open.

## R05e: a delegated holder is told of a request addressed to it

- `AgentMessageService.noticeFromController` files a notice from the controller itself as advice in the holder's inbox, the way an escalation is: it needs no sender principal and no right, so no agent or conversation can use it and the dispatcher's service principal is not widened (the earlier branch hand-built a `service:controller` principal; that was dropped). It is not an API operation.
- The notice names the requesting task and is filed on the parent task, the one the holder holds. It never wakes anyone: the holder reads it at a boundary, a paused or suspended holder keeps it queued (a stopped one, with reach `unavailable`), and it is never an interruption.
- Not lost under backpressure: a full inbox is `unavailable` and stores nothing; the dispatcher's loop `budgets.notifyHolders` (`BudgetService.openForHolders`) tells every holder with an open request on each tick, and filing is idempotent on the command, so a notice that could not be filed, or whose creating call crashed after the commit, is filed on a later tick and never twice. A holder who is not an agent, or can neither read the task nor (when the caller names `admit: budget.manage`, as the budget path does) hold `budget.manage` on it, is skipped (the request stays in `budget.pending` and the owner may decide it); one bad request never holds back the others, and its fault is reported after the rest were tried. Controller notices share the per-sender share of an inbox (`perSenderQueue`), so a requester cannot crowd out a holder's other peer messages (the share is also used by escalations, so a holder with many unread escalations is told of a request late, once it has read some, never lost). A repeat of a request that is already decided tells nobody. Only agent holders are told (a `host:` holder reads `budget.pending`). A request decided between the loop's look and the filing may still get one stale notice; the loop looks at each open request's tree on every tick, which costs more as requests accumulate.
- Deviation from the card text: the notice uses the reserved sender `controller` that escalations already use rather than a provisioned principal record; nothing is forged and no principal gains a right. Recorded for the owner to confirm.
- The retry for a full inbox runs in the dispatcher's tick, so a controller started without a dispatcher retries only when the requester repeats the command.
- Tested: the message service (once, advice, no interruption, paused keeps it queued, refused for a stranger and for a full inbox then filed once there is room), the loop (full inbox retried, forbidden skipped, a real fault surfaces), and the composed controller (told on request, once on repeat, mended by a tick after a lost notice, not announced again once decided); also that a recipient who cannot read the task is refused unless `admit: budget.manage` is named, the per-sender cap, and an unknown `admit` or a non-agent recipient is refused.
- Known limits: the loop scans at most `BUDGET_LIMITS.scan` request records a tick, in storage order (by ID hash, not age), so with more than that many request records an open request past the limit is never found by the loop, and `budget.pending` has the same limit and says `truncated`, so the holder reads each task's `budget.report` for it; the holder is told nothing when its request is decided (the requester finds out by reading its budget).
## H12l and H12d: workspace operations behind the quiesce

- `WorkspaceOpService` (`workspace-ops/`) is the controller's side of integration, checkout refresh and quarantine of a task's work: operations `workspace.request` (`integration`, `refresh`, `quarantine`) and `workspace.get`. The caller needs the new action `workspace.manage` on the task's project, held exactly (a wildcard grant is not enough; the owner always may; a task credential never does; a caller without it reads as `not_found`).
- The request is recorded before anything runs (`workspace-request`, state `started`). The host is asked through `WorkerHost.workspace` (a `WorkspacePort`) only inside `QuiesceCoordinator.around` for the task: every live attempt has new calls refused, calls in flight settled and a checkpoint taken, and is released afterwards whatever the result. If an attempt cannot be made quiet (a failed checkpoint, or a call that ignores the stop signal) the host is not asked and the answer is `refused` with the `runtime_hold` blocker; a host that says no is `refused`; a host that throws is `failed`.
- One operation runs per task at a time in the controller (a second is `unavailable`). The task's live attempts are written into the record before anything is frozen (an attempt that starts later is found by recovery through the task's live attempts and the tag), each freeze carries the request's ID in its reason, and an index record per task names the request that is open on it. A repeat of a command returns the recorded answer; a repeat while the first call is still working is `uncertain` for the repeat (the first call keeps its freeze and writes the real outcome over it). A request left open by a stopped controller is resolved by the dispatcher's `workspace.recover` loop (which reads only the open index) or by the next request for that task, whichever comes first: its own freeze is lifted first (only one that carries its ID, never anybody else's, not even another workspace request's), then it is recorded as `uncertain`, and the operation is never run again.
- A host's summary is cut and redacted; its detail is kept only when it is plain JSON under 4000 bytes (UTF-8) with nothing credential-shaped in it.
- The host is the one that runs the task's live attempt; with no live attempt it is the only host that has a `workspace` port, and with several such hosts and no live attempt it is not found and the request is `refused` (`no host that can do this holds the checkout`).
- Proven here with simulated hosts, through the service and through the state API of the composed controller: the in-flight call settles before the host is asked, nothing is left frozen, the attempt continues, the blocker is typed (checkpoint failure and a call that ignores the stop), rights and replay, concurrency, redaction, crash recovery.
- Known limits, all carried by card H12m: no production host provides a `workspace` port yet (a request is answered `refused`); an attempt that starts while an operation runs is not held back; the agent is not told its checkout changed; a live attempt waiting with no pinned host falls through to the only capable host; `workspacePortOf` is on the handle, so the port can be called without the service (by convention only); the record names the task and requester, not the task's assignee; release (A06) is not wrapped.

- H12l limit carried to H12m: if lifting the freeze fails on the error path of the quiesce (after a refusal or a host fault) no blocker is opened and the record forgets `held`; recovery still finds it by the tag only while the index names the request.
- Not tested: the per-entry error handling of `recover` (one failing task does not stop the others; the first fault is rethrown after the scan).
## U05b: artifact verification and failed handlings in the composed status

- New query `status.ask { request }` puts the status views on the state API (task, overview, noticeboard, changes, tools, delivered, failed events, one failed event), answered by the same `StatusService` the owner chat uses; what the caller may not read reads as missing; a task credential may not ask. The status service is now built whether or not `chat` is given.
- `startController({ artifacts: { directory } })` opens the artifact store for the status (a `FileBlobStore` and `ArtifactService` over the same storage) and gives `StatusService` its `verifyArtifact`. Without it artifacts are shown as `not checked`, never as verified. Opening creates the folder if it is missing, so a mistyped path shows every artifact as not matching; the option is not defaulted from the remote hosts' blob folder.
- Proven through the state API of the started controller: a delivered artifact whose files are intact is reported as checked and matching; one whose file was removed from the store and one whose bytes were replaced are each reported as not matching and not counted as delivered; a seeded failed handling is listed and then inspected (its error and attempts shown), also by `events.failures` and `events.handling`; a reader with `history.read` sees it; a reader with only `task.read` gets an empty failure list, `not_found` for the handling and no artifact lines.
- Known limits: any principal with `artifact.read` can ask for the delivered view, and each ask hashes the files of up to 20 artifacts (a blob may be up to 1 GiB), so the cost is not bounded by the caller; caching the verdict by manifest digest is not done. The failed handling is seeded as a record, not produced by a real delivery failure through the composed controller (that path is proven at service level in the watcher tests); the check reads at most the first 20 artifacts of a project per question (`verifyLimit`); an I/O fault while checking (not a missing or changed file) is shown as not matching, not as not checked.
## P01b: release, per-project lookups, scan limit as a blocker, pin failure

- `checkout.release` (right: `assignment.manage` on the task plus `resource.read`) marks a task's pin released when the task no longer names a repository; refused while it still names one (use `checkout.repin`), for a stale revision, or when nothing is pinned. A released pin holds nothing: it no longer keeps a binding from being unbound, `dispatchCheckout`/`pinCheckout` treat the task as unpinned, and a task that names a repository again is pinned afresh (the pin record is updated, not recreated).
- Each project's `resource-registry` record now lists its binding IDs; `list` and the overlap/uniqueness lookups of that project read only those records. A registry made before the list existed is read once by the old kind-wide scan. A project is capped at the scan limit in bindings (unbound ones count); past it a bind is refused and a read is `unavailable`, never answered from part of the list.
- The dispatcher turns an `unavailable` checkout lookup into the usual typed `dispatch_blocked` blocker (same one each tick) instead of failing the tick quietly. A pin that throws, or a checkout that moved, gives back the place and the budget hold: `#giveBack` re-reads the dispatch record (the caller's copy could miss the request or reservation made in the same advance, which was a stale-request bug in the existing `changed` and budget-refused paths too), moves the hold to `releasingId` (and counts a `reserveRound`) in one write, releases it (`budgets.release`) under a command ID of that round, then clears the mark; a process that stopped in between has the release finished at the start of the next advance, before anything is judged, so an attempt never starts on a hold that was already released, and the next hold gets a new command ID. A release refused as `invalid_transition` (already settled, or held as uncertain) is told through `onError`, not silent. The dispatcher's pin command ID now carries the pin record's revision once a record exists, so pinning after a release is not answered with the first pin's recorded result.
- Known limits (split to card P01c): the overlap check on a new binding (`#checkOverlap`) and the pins-per-binding check (`#liveTasksPinnedTo`, pins are never deleted) still scan kind-wide and report `unavailable` past the limit; moving them to indexes is not done. An agent is not told its pin was released.
- Review fixes: an attempt that already used budget keeps its hold when it is sent back and skipped (the hold carries its use and is settled at the end; `release` is only for a hold that was never used), and ending an attempt finishes a release that was begun and not finished. The old note that a registry without the id list is "read once by the old scan" was wrong: it is scanned on each read until the next bind writes the list.
- Known limits: a hold made just before a crash, before its id was written to the record, is found again only when the same round asks to hold again (the command ID replays it); if the attempt ends first, that hold stays open and shows in the task's report. A failing pin on a waiting attempt is now told in the tick report (`failures`) and retried next tick, without stopping the others.

## M01c: owner time zone and the invitation inbox in the composed controller

- `meeting.timeZone` is now a registered setting in the composed configuration service, and the API's meeting service reads it (`ConfigurationService.installationValue`, a rights-free read for the controller's own use) when a schedule names no zone. The schedule records that the zone came from the setting.
- The dispatcher's meeting service sends invitations to `InvitationInbox` unless the host supplies a sink (then the host delivers them itself and `meeting.invitations` stays empty): one inbox record per agent holding its 50 most recently sent invitations, latest first (older ones drop off); a key delivered twice, even with a changed body, adds nothing. Nothing scans other agents' records, so the inbox cannot run out of room for everyone. `meeting.invitations {agent}` is read by the agent itself (a task credential of that agent too), or by the owner for anyone; every other caller sees an empty list.
- The schedule's zone is fixed when the schedule is made; a later change of the `meeting.timeZone` setting does not move existing schedules.
- Known limits: the inbox is a list the agent must look at; nothing wakes the agent or marks an invitation as read or answered. Pushing them into the agent's conversation or a bounded meeting task is not done.
## M01b: participants withheld in the composed controller

- Defect found and fixed: the dispatcher's own pause service (the instance that decides meeting participants and sends invitations) was built without the host's `availability` hook, so an agent the host reported `suspended` or `stopped` was never withheld there; only the pause gates counted. `startController` now passes `options.availability` into the composed dispatcher.
- Proven through the composed controller with real agent records: a scheduled occurrence marks a paused agent `withheld-paused` and a host-stopped agent `withheld-unavailable` (the available one `eligible`), the pause is not lifted by being withheld, the occurrence takes the open agenda item, and after the occurrence is settled `cancelled` the item is on the open agenda again.
- "Not woken" is shown by a recording invitation sink: only the available agent is invited, and the pause of the paused one stays in force.
## C08b: decisions from the chat, generation interrupted by the dispatcher

- The chat can record a decision: `decision.record` is a chat command (applied at once, shown back), the controller sets `sourceTurnId` to the owner's own turn (the interpreter cannot: that is refused), and the decision service checks the wording is in the owner's own text of that turn. `basedOn` is read from the records (`decision.authoritative`: the current version, 0 when nothing was decided); a topic in dispute is refused with a message to settle the dispute first. Direct callers keep `source: direct`; only the owner may name a turn.
- Defects found: (1) nothing gave the decision service a generation service, so the propagation marked its generation step done without interrupting anything. The API's own instance still has none, so there the task is still told but the generation step is not marked done (the correction stays pending and says so; with no dispatcher running it stays pending, which is the honest state), and the dispatcher's instance, which now has the generation service (filled in after both are built), finishes it from its `decisions.resume` loop. (2) The dispatcher's service principal could neither see the task's generation gate nor correct it (no grants), so even with the service attached nothing was interrupted; the generation service now lets that one principal read gates and carry a correction (not read runs or begin anything).
- Proven through the composed controller on SQLite: a correction recorded through the API leaves the step pending, a restart before the dispatcher ran loses nothing, the dispatcher's tick interrupts the running generation as `corrected`, and what the agent still sends is late and not applied; the same with the task paused.
- Known limit: links, revalidation and the block of dependent work after a restart are covered by the existing service-level tests; this card's composed tests cover the generation step and the pause and restart only.
- Review fixes: the version a chat decision is based on is the newest live version that applies to its scope (a task-level decision counts for a project-wide one), counted ahead within one message by the normalised topic, so "PostgreSQL, then SQLite instead" in one message supersedes rather than disputes; the interpreter cannot name `basedOn` or `session` (refused), and `gate`/`stance`/`session` are no longer exempt from the own-words check. A decision that is not a decision (a question) records nothing and the owner is told "Nothing was recorded: ..." instead of "Done". The earlier API decision test is kept (the generation test is its own file).
- Known limits: a decision resumed after the owner answers a clarifying question takes the answering turn as its source and is refused when its wording is in the original turn (it fails closed); `decision.record` applies at once in every profile, including strict (the owner's own words are the authority; whether a chat gate or correction should be shown first in strict is an owner decision).
- C08b third review: the decisions of one message are counted ahead by scope (a project-wide one applies to all, a task's own to that task and the project-wide ones), so two decisions for different tasks do not dispute each other; a decision that became a dispute says so, and "Nothing was recorded" is the whole answer for a non-decision (no "Done"). Known gap for the owner: a gate cannot be set from the chat unless its word (for instance implementation-hold) is in the message, because the interpreter's gate choice is no longer exempt from the own-words check (it would apply a project-wide hold on the interpreter's word alone); whether to allow chat gates as a proposal is an owner question. The note that `basedOn` comes from `decision.authoritative` is superseded: it comes from the topic's history for the decision's scope.
- C08b fourth round: the version an applied decision is based on is now read when the step is applied (after the earlier steps of the message), not predicted from the plan; the earlier prediction was wrong whenever an earlier step recorded nothing (a restatement) or wrote for another scope, since versions count the whole topic. The prediction stays only for a proposal that waits for the owner, where the stale check is the point. A chat gate needs the gate word and the topic name (implementation-gate) in the owner's own words; this is part of the owner question. Saying the same decision twice in one message is a restatement and records nothing the second time.
- C08b fifth round: a turn run again (crash, or sent twice at once) answers an already recorded decision of its own as applied, with the record's version in the reply, and a `command_conflict` from a copy that raced is answered the same way when the record is this turn's. Known limit (owner may want it closed): a step not recorded before a crash of its turn (one refused at apply time, the step that crashed, and every later one) is read afresh on replay; replayed after the owner changed the topic meanwhile, it reads the base version afresh and can overwrite that change instead of becoming a dispute. Closing it needs the plan-time version kept and the fresh one used only when every newer entry is this turn's own.

- (Partly superseded by the third review below: the handle now names its placement, the checkpoint wait re-checks it, and a startup failure closes the host.) Known limits recorded for card H02b (second review): the placement check in the handle is check-then-act (`control()` takes no placement number, so a move committing between the check and the control call lands the old handle's message in the new placement); the checkpoint wait does not re-check the placement and a new host's checkpoint can satisfy an old handle's wait (the sequence carries over a move); a failure of `FileBlobStore.open` or remote-service construction after the local host was built still leaves that host open.

## H02b (part): startup failures, placement-numbered control, visible refusals

- Any step that fails after the local host was built (the artifact folder, remote service, listener, dispatcher, MCP) now closes the listener and the local host before the error leaves `composeDispatch` (before, only a listener failure did; the controller starts without a dispatcher and `dispatchProblem` says why). Tested for an unopenable artifact folder and a taken port, and that the controller's own close does not close the host a second time.
- `RemoteWorkerService.control` takes the caller's placement number and refuses (`fenced`) in the same commit that would write the message if another placement holds the attempt; the production handle passes its own for checkpoint, restart and tell. The checkpoint wait now stops with `fenced` when the placement moved, so the wait ends `fenced` once a move is visible (a move and a new-host checkpoint landing between the wait's last check and the read of the latest checkpoint is a tiny window that is not closed). Tested in the relocation suite.
- A host that cannot meet an attempt's requirements: the dispatcher's report now says why (`the worker did not start: <reason>`), not only the attempt's end record; tested through the composed controller (an isolation the host does not offer).
- Not done, split to card H02c: partition and delayed-packet fencing, no self-promotion, relocation with integrity and policy refusals, the exclusive native-store owner, and the production host's stop path, each through the composed controller.
- Review fixes (third review): the production handle is tested through a stale view of the placement (the fence in the commit refuses `tell`, `restart` and `checkpoint`) and the checkpoint wait ends `fenced` when the placement moved; the driver is started last, after everything that can fail, so a failed start leaves none ticking. Still untested: closing the listener after it was opened when a later step fails (both startup tests fail at or before `listen`); it is the first item of H02c, together with a failure injected into the driver or MCP construction (the driver is started last so none ticks after a failed start, which is untested).
## R05d (part): meeting time is charged

- When an agent leaves a meeting (by itself or at the end), the time it was present is charged to the budget ledger: `AttendanceDeps.charge`, composed in `dispatch-compose.ts` as `budgets.charge` under the dispatcher's principal, activity `meeting`. The basis is stated: wall-clock milliseconds between joining and leaving, recorded as compute (`computeMs`), never as money. It goes to the agent's meeting task (work) or, with none, to the shared-overhead rule "meeting" (an agent that joined always has a meeting task, so in practice this branch is only a fallback and is not reached or tested).
- Once only: the command ID is the attendance's (`att-use:<attendance>`), so a repeated leave replays the same charge. The owner's presence is not charged (tested: the check is on the agent identity, "agent:..."). A failing ledger is reported (`onChargeError`, the composed `onError`) and never keeps the agent in the room; a later `leave` of the same attendance charges it (the end of the meeting does not retry, because it skips those who have left).
- Not done, split to R05f: supervision and review activity, background jobs (the job service is not yet composed in the controller), and a composed proof through the state API that a held meeting appears in `budget.usage` (the unit test uses the service seam only). A charge lost because the ledger stayed down is not found again by a sweep.
- Possible double count to check in R05f: if an agent's meeting turns are ever dispatched as attempts on its meeting task, their model-call use settles against that same task as well as this wall-clock charge.

## P01c: pin lists and the overlap check without kind-wide scans

- Each binding has a pin list (`resource-pins`, made with the binding): the tasks whose checkout is or was pinned to it. Ending a binding reads that list (checking each task still points there and is not finished), not every checkout of every project, and its commit checks the list at the revision it read, so a pin that commits meanwhile makes the unbind fail and the binding stays bound. Pin, repin (moves the task between two lists) and release keep the list in the same commit as the checkout. A list is cleared of finished tasks once it holds 50 (or the scan limit, if lower); past the scan limit in live pins a pin is refused as `unavailable` (field `pins`).
- A binding made before the list existed has none. Its first pin starts a list marked `legacy` without looking at older checkouts (the pin never scans), and ending a binding with no list or a `legacy` one also looks through the checkouts (refused as `unavailable` past the scan limit, never answered from part); ending a list-less binding leaves a legacy empty list so a pin racing it conflicts.
- The overlap check reads each project's registry, which now also holds the bound locations of the project (`locs`, kept by bind, move and unbind; a registry without them is read from its bindings and gets them at its next change). The limit counts projects, not bindings. The check still looks across projects by nature (an overlap is between projects), so it is a scan of the project registries.
- A task whose pin the list could not take is a blocker: the dispatcher's look (before any place or allowance is taken) tests the pin list's capacity and answers `unbound` with the reason, which becomes the usual `dispatch_blocked` blocker (the same one each tick). If the limit is reached between that look and the pin, the pin gives the place back and the attempt is skipped for the tick. Only this refusal is mapped so; a store fault in a pin stays a fault.
- Known limits: the project registries are scanned on every bind and move (one record per project); a registry made before P01b (no id list) is still read from all resources for each bind and move until its project next changes a binding; an overlap race between two projects binding at the same moment is not serialized (as before); two pins on one binding at the same moment conflict (one is retried on the next tick; the message says the project's resources changed); pin lists keep finished tasks until a list reaches its clearing size; the `legacy` mark is never cleared, so ending a binding made before the lists existed always looks through the checkouts (as before this card); the look before dispatch reads each task of a long pin list on every tick for a waiting task.

## C08d: a replayed decision step never overwrites a change made meanwhile

- Planning a decision step now records the version of its topic as the message saw it (`planBase`, before any step of the message). When the step is applied, if a decision on the topic that is not from this turn has a higher version than `planBase` (someone changed it after the message was planned), the step is based on `planBase` alone (not adding what this turn recorded: that may have been written in a narrower scope that never saw the change), so the decision service records it as a dispute and the change stands. Otherwise the step is based on the topic as it is now, as before. Disputed topics are still refused before this.
- Proven: a message of two steps whose second step crashes, the owner changes the topic directly, and the message is sent again: the second step is a dispute, nothing is in force until the owner chooses, and the owner's change is not superseded. Removing the rule makes the test fail.
- Review fix: an earlier version added this turn's own newest version to `planBase`, which let a project-wide step overwrite a change that an earlier task-scoped step of the same turn had not seen; tested (replay with a task-scoped then a project-wide step and a change for another task meanwhile).
- Known limit: a decision step reads the topic's history twice at plan time and twice at apply time (cost only); a change between the plan and the first run (no crash) is the same case and the same rule, with no test of its own.

## C08c: chat gates and strict-profile decisions are shown first

- Owner answers (2026-10-27): a gate set from the chat is shown as a proposal the owner confirms, and `decision.record` in the strict profile is shown first; the other profiles still apply a decision at once. `proposalReason` gives the reason ("a gate holds or releases work until you say otherwise, so it is shown first"; "the strict profile shows a recorded decision first"). A profile that cannot be read is strict.
- Because a gate is always seen first, its kind and its fixed topic (`implementation-gate`, set by the controller) no longer have to be words of the owner's message; the gate's wording still has to be (the decision service checks it against the turn), so a gate whose words the owner did not say is still refused. This replaces the C08b rule that a chat gate needed the gate word and the topic name in the owner's words.
- Applying the proposal records the decision from the same turn; its `basedOn` is the version read when the message was planned, so a topic that moved meanwhile becomes a dispute (the stale-session check).
- Review fixes: (1) the preview of a decision says its category and gate first (a long text or task label cannot push the kind off the line) and the recorded line names the gate; (2) a decision proposed from a message is based, when the owner says yes, on the version it was shown with, and decisions of the same message applied before it do not count as the topic having moved (they supersede, in the strict profile too); a change by anyone else in between is still a dispute; a step already recorded is answered from the record when the apply is run again; (3) words that are not a decision (a question, a hypothetical) are not offered for confirmation: the owner is told "Nothing was recorded: ...".
- Known limits: the decision suite now runs in the `derived` profile so that its tests of recording at once stay meaningful; the strict case has its own test.

## R05f: review and job time is charged to the task

- `ReviewOptions.onUsage` is called after an agent reviewer's allow or deny with the wall-clock time from the review's assignment to its decision (`latencyMs` of the route), keyed `review-use:<review>`; escalations, requests for context and the owner's own decisions are not charged. `JobOptions.onUsage` is called when a job ends (finish, a stop that was obeyed, a reconciliation, a restart decision of "complete") with the time from admission to its end, keyed `job-use:<job>`, for background and foreground jobs alike. Both are called again if the same command is repeated, and the key makes the dispatcher's `budgets.charge` count them once.
- Composed: `DispatchHandle.chargeUse` charges through the dispatcher's budget service (activity `review` or `background-job`, to the task); `start.ts` passes it to both services and reports a failed charge through `onInternalError` without undoing the review or the job. Without a dispatcher nothing is charged. Proof: `api/start-usage.test.ts` (a background job ending twice is one entry in `budget.usage`).
- Supervision: the safety supervisor and other supervising agents work as attempts, which settle as model-call use; no separate supervision charge exists to make, so `supervision` stays a reserved activity name for host use. The meeting double count flagged under R05d does not arise: meeting turns are not dispatched as attempts on the meeting task.
- Known limits: the time is wall-clock, so a review left waiting with its reviewer paused counts as used; a job that ended while the dispatcher was not composed (or the ledger was down) is not charged later by a sweep; the owner's review time is not money or compute and is not charged.
- Review fixes: tests now pin each way a job ends (a stop that was obeyed, a reconciliation, a restart decision of complete; a stop that was not obeyed, restart, exception and a request to cancel charge nothing) and an agent reviewer's allow through the composed controller into `budget.usage` as `review` with the reviewer. Behaviour worth knowing: a job cancelled while only admitted is charged its admitted time; a restarted job is charged from its first admission to its final end (downtime and time outcome-unknown included); foreground jobs are booked under `background-job`; a charge that failed while the ledger was down is not retried by anything (split to R05g, with the held-meeting proof through budget.usage).

## H02c (part): fencing, relocation and the store owner through the composed controller

- `DispatchHandle.remote` exposes the remote-worker service of a composed controller (owner moves, placement records); it is composition-internal like the rest of the handle.
- `api/start-remote.test.ts`: a failure injected after the listener opened (in the driver's options, in the MCP options) leaves the port refusing connections, no timer asked for and the local host closed once.
- `api/start-remote-fencing.test.ts` (real worker client over the controller's own transport, the controller's clock moved by the test): a worker silent past its lease is lost and every late heartbeat, checkpoint and result is refused `fenced` and changes nothing (the lost attempt stays abandoned; an accept with a higher placement number than offered is refused); a move is refused by the data-location policy and by a checkpoint whose bytes were changed, each leaving the placement, the store and the old host untouched, then goes through when whole: the old host is fenced on every message, its late checkpoint does not replace the handed-on one, the store follows, the same command is the same move, and the new host is offered the attempt with the checkpoint; the native store keeps a second task of the agent waiting (no blocker) until the first ends, then runs it on the same host, and only the owner moves a store.
- Review fixes: the host order is arranged so the tests depend on the store pin and the move, not on which host comes first; the listener test records that a server was listening when the injected failure happened; the move is checked to restart the new host from exactly the checkpoint the old host sent, a repeat after the new host took it up is answered without a second move, the policy refusal is matched by its reason, a host the attempt is not placed on cannot accept it, a host cannot move a store and the owner can once no attempt holds it.
- Not done, split to H02d: the production host's stop path through the composed controller (a stop reaches a remote worker's poll and ends the attempt), a new host's checkpoint never answering an old handle's request (the dispatcher's checkpoint wait; proved at the service seam in `relocation.test.ts`), the rest of the self-promotion clauses (a worker has no route that admits work, unknown request fields refused) and relocation refusals by platform and workspace paths and the credential policy (service seam only).

## M01d: a lead before each meeting: made and invited early, agents kept free, idle ones nudged

- Setting `meeting.leadMinutes` (whole minutes 0 to 60; unset means 5 in the composed controller, 0 where no reader is composed). The dispatcher instance reads it at the start of each meeting tick: a scheduled meeting's occurrence, and so its invitations, is made at the longer of the schedule's own preparation time and the lead before the start (the `prepareFrom` of a stand-up is unchanged). Urgent meetings are made at once, as before. A setting that cannot be read counts as 0.
- Admission: from `leadMinutes` before a meeting that an agent will attend (reachable, or paused with the owner's direct invitation), new work for that agent is deferred until the meeting ends whatever its expected length, and even work that could yield at a boundary; only a safe long-running operation carries on. Work already running is not touched or stopped. Before the lead the earlier rule stands (work that would still be running at the start waits). With 0 nothing changes.
- Nudge: `dispatch.nudge` (host option) is called after an invitation is in the agent's inbox, for an agent with no running attempt (`liveAttemptsOf`, then the attempt's state); a busy agent is not nudged and finds its invitation at its next stopping point. A failing hint or busy check is reported through `onInternalError` and does not lose the invitation. It is called again if the invitation is delivered again (the key is the invitation's key, so the host can drop repeats). It applies to the controller's own inbox and to a host-supplied invitation sink alike.
- Known limits: what the host does with a nudge (waking a stopped agent, starting a conversation) is the host's; the controller does not wake suspended or stopped agents. The lead is installation-wide, not per project or schedule. The stored `nextPrepareAt` of a schedule is computed with the lead in force when it was written.
- Review fixes: the hint is no longer waited for (a hint that never returns held up the other invitations and the whole tick); busy means an attempt running now (one waiting for a place or parked on an approval is idle and is kept free and nudged); the API instance of the meeting service reads the lead too, so a schedule's `nextPrepareAt` shown to the owner includes it; the admission cap on the lead is the setting's own maximum (60).
- Still true, by design or later: in the tick where the clock first crosses the lead, admission runs before the loop that makes the occurrence, so short work for an invited agent can still start in that one tick; the lead ends a once-only schedule and fixes the day's meeting earlier (by the lead) than before, so an edit in the last minutes before the meeting is refused or skipped; the busy path (a running attempt suppressing the hint) is covered by the unit test of `withNudge` with a fake check, not through a composed running attempt.

## A07d: the length of a standing grant is offered, chosen by the system or by the owner

- A proposal now carries `lengthOptions` (1, 7, 30 and 90 days, `GRANT_LENGTHS`) and `defaultLength` (days and the reason in plain words); `suggestion.days` is the default. The default is `chooseStandingLength`, in this order: a length the owner stated in words (as stated, at most 90); one-off work (1 day); earlier standing grants of the same class that have ended (one taken back early: the next shorter option than the shortest such; ones that ran their full term and were asked for again: the next longer than the longest); the span of the approvals the proposal is drawn from (the shortest option that covers it); otherwise the 30 days of A07b. It never exceeds 90.
- `accept` takes `days` (an explicit length, whole days up to 90, used exactly), or `statedDays` and `oneOff` (what the owner said or marked, derived again with them), or nothing (the default shown). `days` cannot be combined with the others. The length and how it was chosen (`chosenLength`: days, `owner` or `default`, the reason) are written in the same step that accepts, so a retry after a failure makes the same grant; the grant expires that many days after the acceptance and its basis carries the reason; `accept` returns the days and the reason. The profile-switch answer (`acceptBySwitching`) is unchanged and is the other answer to the same proposal.
- A class the policy reserves, an unclassified one and the classes that stay decisions are still never proposed (unchanged from A07b).
- Not done: the state API and chat do not offer the length choice yet (no approval operation exists in the state API; U08 shows proposals), so turning words like "for a week" into `statedDays` is the caller's job; the explanation is kept on the proposal and in the grant's basis, and C09 will capture it with the other decision explanations (the card no longer waits for C09). "How long earlier grants stayed in use" is read as whether they ran to their end or were taken back; actual use of a grant is not recorded per grant. Earlier grants are found by listing every proposal (200 a page).
- **Review fixes (Opus).** (1) A proposal stored before this card (no `defaultLength`) is accepted at the length it showed (`suggestion.days`, "the usual length"), never at a newly derived one. (2) A grant revoked after its term counts as having run its full term: `GrantService.revoke` now records `revokedAt`; a revocation with no time (older grants) counts as early. (3) The earlier-grant history is kept on the proposal itself (`history`, at most 5, oldest first, with `spanDays`) and so is only the same requester, project, class and environment; it survives a re-offer the owner dismissed; the latest entry alone decides (taken back: shorter than that length; ran its term: longer). `propose` no longer scans proposals (the cost finding) and `accept` never scans. (4) The owner's words (`statedDays`, `oneOff`) are recorded with source `owner`. (5) The accept payload leaves out parameters not given, so a retry from before the upgrade replays; an accepted proposal with no grant yet is finished at its fixed length whatever length the retry names. (6) Span rounding: the shortest option at least the exact span (7.01 days gives 30), the text says "about N days"; wording "N-day term"; `oneOff: false` with `days` is fine; the `days` error names 1 to 90 (`statedDays` allows up to 3650 and is cut to 90). Open question for the owner: `statedDays` is used as the exact length (the card calls the words "a limit"); a span of under a day (the usual case for three quick approvals) gives a 1-day grant.


## V01b — stall thresholds follow the prompt size and the model's measured speed

- `request_started` may carry `promptTokens` (an estimate: the body's characters over 3 per token, rounded up), `cachedShare`, `route` and `hostId`. New events `first_output` (ends the reading allowance, counts as progress, a repeat does not move it) and `output_progress` (token count so far; only grows; implies output has begun). `request_finished` may carry the provider's `inputTokens`, `cachedTokens`, `outputTokens`.
- `assessStall` takes an optional `reading` (speed, source, margin). While a request has a prompt estimate and no output, the allowed time is `max(difficulty requestMs, margin × expected reading time)`; the same allowance lifts the `silent` limit. The `stuck_request` text then states the prompt size, the speed used and where it came from (measured, declared, default), the time expected and the time allowed. A request with no estimate is judged as before.
- Speed per route and host is kept in `stall-speed` records (`StallService.speed`, owner or service only), smoothed (70% old, 30% new) with each sample bounded to half and double the old value; a sample counts only when ≥ 200 tokens read over ≥ 1 s (or ≥ 20 tokens written over ≥ 1 s), the request succeeded and had a first output. Cached tokens are subtracted before reading speed is taken.
- Order of speed used: measured → declared (`declaredSpeed(route, host)` option) → `defaultReadTokensPerSecond` (50). `readMarginPercent` defaults to 150. Both are validated and can be given through `StartOptions.stall` (with `thresholds`).
- The relay has a `RelayMonitor` (started / firstOutput / progress at most every `progressMs`, default 15 s / finished with counts). Probes (`count_tokens`) are not monitored; a reply the reader leaves part way is reported as failed once. The composer sends these to `StallService.reportFromRelay`, one after another per attempt; a fenced or vanished task is dropped quietly. The evidence keeps the worker's own `reportedBy`.
- Not done (split to V01c): reading the declared speed from the route settings in the routing table, and the cache adapter's expected cached share on `request_started`. Until then a route is declared through `StartOptions.stall.declaredSpeed`, and the whole estimate counts (the safe side is a longer allowance only when a prompt is large).
- **Review fixes (Opus).** (1) The relay monitor's `started` returns a handle for that call only, so overlapping calls (Pi retrying while the first call is still being read) are never mixed up. (2) `reportFromRelay` also takes the attempt ID and is fenced unless it is the assignment's active attempt (attempts of a generation share it). (3) SSE comments and ping events are not output: only the first real data ends the reading allowance or counts as progress. Not handled: a role-only first chunk counts as output. (4) Anthropic cache creation is read work (in the input total, not in the cached part); only cache reads are cached. (5) New tests: a lost first-output event, a repeat not moving the time, the relay keeping the worker as reporter, attempt fencing, and a relayed call writing a speed record through the composed controller. Known and left: `output_progress.tokens` is a byte estimate (stream bytes over 3), the provider's count replaces it at the end; the relay sends no host ID, so speeds are kept per route and `-` until the relay knows the host (V01c); a reply body that is never read reports no end and the request stays open until the next one starts; the per-attempt serial queue is not pinned by a test.
- **Second review (PASS) leftovers.** The composer drops only the "is not the open request" refusal (an overlapped call's late end), fenced and not_found quietly; other validation errors go to `onError`. A keep-alive split across two network pieces counts as output; the attempt fence is checked before the report's transaction (a window of one report).


## T09 — command namespaces and alias dispatch

- New `commands/` module. `parseInvocation` accepts `/<namespace>.<name> rest` only in the lower-case ASCII grammar (namespaces `nimblenewt`, `toolbox`, `a_<id>`, and the aliases `agent`, `custom`); case, encodings, Unicode look-alikes, extra dots and over-long names are refused, never normalised.
- `CommandResolver` (over a `CommandSource`; `catalogSource(CatalogService)` is the real one, so what a caller can see is what the catalog lets them see) gives `resolved` (a `Target`: `operationId` = canonical name, layer, version, digest, schema digest, owner id, display name, all separate), `ambiguous`, `needs_context`, `unknown` or `refused`. A namespace whose catalog layer disagrees is refused, so nothing filed under `nimblenewt.` or `toolbox.` by anyone else runs as one. Typed commands, `resolveWire` (`<ns>__<name>`) and `resolveAction` end in the same target.
- `/agent.<name>` needs the explicitly selected agent (by immutable ID; a friendly name is refused). With none selected it never picks one: two or more agents with the command are `ambiguous`, one is `needs_context` (the shortcut must not mean "whoever is the only one today").
- `/custom.<name>` resolves only in an explicit scope through aliases the owner defines (`CommandService.defineAlias` / `removeAlias` / `aliases`). An alias names one canonical command, never another alias, grants nothing, cannot silently be overwritten (remove, then define), and a removed name is unknown in that scope.
- `CommandService.enqueue` resolves and, only when resolved, stores a `queued-command` with the target, the arguments as typed (redacted, bounded) and the context; the shortcut is kept for display. It resolves again inside the command, so a retry never queues something else. Owner or agent may queue; the requester or owner reads it. Whether the caller may run the command is decided where it runs.
- Not done (split to T09b): wiring the catalog and commands into `startController`, the state API and the chat; executing queued commands; friendly-name display for agents. The catalog itself is not yet a controller service in `start.ts`.
- **Review fixes (Opus).** The stored `typed` text is redacted like the arguments. A retry of a queued command is answered from its record (marked replayed) even when the name no longer resolves; the same command ID with other text or context is a conflict (`asked` digest). A `/custom.` alias whose target the caller cannot see answers like an alias that does not exist, so it reveals neither the alias nor whose command it names. Pins added for agent removal of aliases and a non-owner/agent queueing. Deferred to T09b with the wiring: `/toolbox.` resolves globally (the spec asks for an explicit toolbox scope), the scope string is the caller's word until it is tied to grants, `displayName` is the command name until agents and tools carry labels, and execution must check permissions where the command runs.

## H07 — idle host polling and capability placement

- **One held poll per host.** `GET /worker/session/offers?wait=<ms>` (0 to `REMOTE_LIMITS.pollMs` = 25 000; any other parameter or value is refused). With no offer waiting, the controller holds the request until an offer is made to that host (`place`), the host's session is replaced (the held poll then ends `fenced`), a newer poll of the same host takes over (the earlier one ends empty), `RemoteWorkerService.close()` runs, or the time is up. A host never has two held polls; an idle host costs one open request. `pollStats` (owner/dispatcher) shows open, total, held, woken, superseded and timed-out polls.
- **`HostPoller`** (worker side, `remote/poller.ts`): one per host, never one per agent or attempt. It connects (the first connection after a start waits a random part of `spreadMs`), sends heartbeats on their own interval and never holds a poll past the next heartbeat, hands offers to `onOffers`, and keeps at least `minGapMs` between polls so a controller that answers at once cannot make a request loop. Failures back off with full jitter (random in 0 to `min(max, base * 2^(n-1))`), reset after a success; a fenced session is dropped and connected again; a refused protocol (426), a bad credential (401/403) waits the longest backoff; `rate_limited` honours a floor. Sleep, random and clock are injected.
- **Capability-indexed placement.** The service keeps connected hosts by platform (`os/arch`); `candidates(by, query)` looks only at hosts of the platform the attempt needs (`considered` counts them), judges each by its announced capabilities, freshness, session and the placement policy, orders the eligible by fewest un-accepted offers then host ID, lists why the others cannot (at most 20), and when none can says in words what is connected and that the attempt waits (`waiting`). The index fills at connect and at the first poll after a controller restart.
- **Placement policy** (`RemoteDeps.placementPolicy`, hook absent in the product by default; local-only data is then never placed remotely): `credentialHosts` (empty/absent = any), `dataHosts` , `repositoryHosts`. `place` refuses an ineligible host with every reason and so never puts the task credential into an offer for it; the dispatcher's start on such a host is skipped with those reasons. Pure `policyReasons`.
- **Limits changed:** the transport's per-address allowance is 3000 requests a minute (was 1200) and 250 connections per address (was 100): a site's hosts often share one address and every idle host holds a connection. At the default 20 s hold and 15 s heartbeat a host makes 7 requests a minute. Measured in the test: 100 idle hosts on the reference store hold 95-100 polls and make about two or three polls each in 6 s with a 3 s hold, none superseded. Each poll costs a few store reads on the controller.
- **Not done:** the dispatcher does not yet choose among hosts with `candidates` or fall back to the next host when a placement is refused (it is still the order of `workers`, H12a); a poller for the product host process (the worker package) is not wired; no jitter on the controller side of a mass reconnect other than the pollers' own.
- **Review fixes (Opus):** (1) a lost wakeup: an offer made between a poll's read and its wait is now caught by a per-host counter (the read is repeated, not waited out); the test starts polls at several offsets against the making of an offer but cannot pin the microtask window over HTTP, so that guard is not mutation-proven. (2) `placementPolicy` is plumbed through `RemoteStartOptions`, and with no policy hook `local-only` data is never placed on a remote host (it was open); the test world defaults to listing its hosts, `placement: null` is the product default. (3) The 100-host test now runs inside the default transport limits (per-address 3000/min) and includes a reconnect burst (all sessions replaced; pollers fenced, reconnect, polls held again, nothing refused as too many requests). (4) The poller counts a failing `onOffers` as a failure (no reset, backoff grows, minGap always applies); refused-outright hosts wait 75-100% of the longest backoff (jittered). (5) `close()` sets a flag so later polls are not held, and the composed `closeWorkers` calls it. Left: a poll is not ended when its client disconnects (it ends at its wait), `onTrouble` reports every failure as `poll`, `rate_limited` floors at 1 s rather than reading `retry-after`, aborting the poller waits out a held poll, the platform index keeps revoked hosts in `considered` and is filled at a restart only at a host's first poll, and the policy is checked at `place`, not again at delivery. Per-address 250 connections against a global 1000 lets four addresses fill the listener: owner question.

## Batch closing (2026-10-27): P01c, C08d, C08c, M01d, R05f, H02c, T09, H07 flipped
- Flipped on exhaustive CI run 40591614995 (commit b651702, green on all 18 jobs). Earlier exhaustive runs failed only on timing assumptions in the H07 polling tests (fixed sleeps on slow Windows runners) and on generated plan docs that had not been regenerated; both fixed, tests now wait on conditions.
- A07d and V01b were flipped afterwards, once the owner decided to drop their C09 and H12b/H12e edges.
- New cards: R05g, H02d, V01c, T09b, H07b, H02e (all in D03's dependencies).
- **Owner answers (2026-10-27):** drop the C09 edge from A07d, H12b/H12e from V01b and G04 from X11 (X11 now depends on G01 so the plan keeps one root); a stated number of days stays the exact length; the suggested standing-grant length after a short burst is at least seven days (A07e); local-only placement follows the profile, strict lists hosts and the other profiles allow the owner's enrolled hosts, changeable by chat as a proposal (H07c); connection limits per address apply only before login (H07d).

## A07e — at least seven days suggested
- After a burst of approvals the suggested standing-grant length is `max(option that covers the span, 7 days)`, worded "N days is the least suggested, so you are not asked again within a week". The shorter options stay listed, the lengths after a revoked or full-term grant are unchanged, and a stated number of days is still the exact length. Mutation: removing the floor fails the new assertions.

## H02e — a poll no longer deletes a re-placed offer
- `#pending` judged the offer it read before an await against the placement stored after it, and deleted on a mismatch, so an attempt placed again meanwhile lost its new offer until the lease ended. It now compares with the offer held after the read: a newer offer is returned if its placement is stored as offered, and only the offer that was read is ever deleted. The test stalls the poll's read of the placement, places the attempt again, and checks the new offer survives; restoring the old logic fails it.

## H07d — connection limits apply per address only before login
- A new `ConnectionBook` counts a connection against the stranger pools (`connectionsPerAddress`, default 100, and `connections` in all, default 400) until its first authenticated request, then against its host (`connectionsPerHost`, default 8). Logged-in hosts behind one address are no longer limited as strangers (the 250/1000 of H07 is replaced; the listener's room for logged-in hosts is 8 per enrolled host, so it grows with them), and strangers can fill only their own pool. A host past its own allowance is answered `rate_limited` with `connection: close`.
- Known limit: a login burst (many hosts connecting at once from one address) counts as strangers until each first request authenticates, so more than 100 simultaneous new connections from one address have some dropped; the poller's backoff and jitter retry them. A pool filled by strangers also keeps a new host from connecting until they leave (over plain HTTP a silent socket gets a 408 after the headers timeout plus the check interval, up to about 40 s; over TLS the HTTP timers start only after the handshake, so a socket that never finishes one holds its place until the TLS handshake timeout, 120 s by default); hosts already connected keep their connections. `WorkerTransport.connectionCounts()` shows both pools. Mutations (no host cap, no login promotion, no release of the stranger count) fail the transport test. Review fix: over TLS the request's socket wraps the accepted one, so the book now looks up the accepted socket (`_parent`); a TLS variant of the test, a reconnect-many-times test (host places are released on close) and an exact-boundary check (a closed connection frees its place) pin it.

## R05g — lost charges are retried; a held meeting is proved through budget.usage
- `ChargeRetryService` (`budgets/retry.ts`): the dispatcher's charges for reviews, jobs and meeting presence go through `submit`. A charge that books at once is not kept. One that fails for a reason that may pass (ledger or store down, a lost race) is kept as a `charge-retry` record with a due time; a charge that is wrong in itself (`invalid_command`, `not_found`, `forbidden`, `unauthenticated`) throws to the caller as before. A dispatcher loop `charge-retry` calls `sweep` each tick: due charges are tried (at most 50 a sweep, from the index of waiting charges) with the delay doubling from 5 s to an hour; a charge is given up on after 20 tries or at once if it turns out wrong, and `onDropped` reports it through `onInternalError`. The charge's own command ID is the budget key, so a try that landed but lost its answer books once. `unsettled(by)` (owner or dispatcher) lists pending and given-up charges; `DispatchHandle.unsettledCharges` and `DispatchHandle.attendance` are exposed.
- Proof: `budgets/retry.test.ts` (21 tests on the three backends; doubling, cap, give-up, wrong charges, bounded sweeps, access) and `api/start-usage.test.ts` (an agent joins and leaves a held meeting, twice; one `meeting` entry of 7 minutes on the meeting task, in `budget.usage`, and the retry loop runs in the tick). Mutations (no doubling, no give-up, permanent errors kept, due time ignored, unbounded sweep, loop removed) fail.
- A single `charge-retry-index/pending` record lists the waiting charges, changed in the same commit as each charge record, so a sweep reads only those and settled or given-up records never slow it. Limits: settled and dropped records stay (no delete exists); a failure to even keep a charge (store down too) is reported and the charge is lost; the composed controller has no way to make the ledger fail, so the retry is proved at the service seam and the loop's presence in the tick.

### R05g review fixes
- Charges that failed together raced for the one index record and the loser was reported dropped (probe: 10 parallel submits kept 1). A keep now rebuilds its change from the newer index and tries again (up to 30 rounds with a short random wait); a test submits ten at once and expects none dropped. The test also pins that booked and given-up charges leave the index (a mutation that never shrinks it fails).
- Known and left: a charge given up on and later failing again under the same command ID is not queued a second time (the earlier record stays); `unsettled` reads every kept record, settled ones included, until a later card prunes them.

## V01c — declared model speed from the routing table, and the expected cache share
- A route in the routing table may carry `readTokensPerSecond` and `writeTokensPerSecond` (numbers above 0, at most 1 000 000; validated with the table). The composed controller gives stall detection a `declaredSpeed` that uses a speed given in `StartOptions.stall` first, else the table's `readTokensPerSecond` for that route, until the route has been measured; `StallOptions.declaredSpeed` may now be asynchronous. The write speed is stored in the table for display and later use; nothing reads it yet.
- The relay's `request_started` now carries `cachedShare`: the share of the prompt the cache served on the attempt's latest finished successful call (cached over input tokens), which the next call, repeating most of that prompt, is expected to match. The first call of an attempt has none. This is the attempt's own observation, not a prediction from the cache adapter's slot or pin state (the adapter reports figures only after a call).
- Proof: `api/start-stall-relay.test.ts` (a routing table declaring 20 tokens a second: the first call's assessment says `declared`, 20; the next call opens with `cachedShare` 0.75; a zero speed is refused). Removing the table lookup or the share fails it.

## H07c — local-only placement follows the approval profile; the owner changes it in chat
- `PlacementSettingsService` (`remote/placement-settings.ts`) keeps one owner-written record: hosts to `allow` and to `exclude`. `dataHostsFor(profile, settings, enrolledHosts)` gives who may hold `local-only` data: **strict** only the allowed hosts (minus the excluded); **derived and autonomous** every enrolled, active host of the owner plus the allowed, minus the excluded; a profile that cannot be read is strict. The profile is read from the installation's approval-policy record at every placement, so a profile or setting change counts from the next placement.
- State API: `placement.get` (query, owner only: allow, exclude, profile, the hosts that may hold local-only data now, revision) and `placement.set` (command, owner only; each list replaces the earlier one, one left out stays; `expectedRevision` optional). Chat: `placement.set` is a `propose` command, so it is shown first in every profile and applies only on the owner's word; the chat refuses host names the owner did not write. Cloud-allowed data is unaffected.
- Composed: `startController` gives the remote service this policy unless the operator passed a `remote.placementPolicy` of their own. Proof: `api/start-placement.test.ts` (strict lists none; an allowed host counts at once; stale revision, bad names and other principals refused; derived allows all three enrolled hosts; an exclusion removes one; the chat proposal changes nothing until applied) and `remote/placement-settings.test.ts`. Mutations (profile branch, wiring, exclusions) fail.
- Not done: credential and repository host lists are still only the operator's `placementPolicy`; the setting names hosts, not groups; a revoked host leaves the derived list only because it is no longer active.

### H07c review fixes
- The chat now proposes `placement.change` (add or remove hosts, the rest of the lists untouched) instead of replacing whole lists: a "don't let host:laptop hold my files" can no longer undo an earlier exclusion, and a proposal that waits while the setting changes does only what it says (test: another host is excluded meanwhile and stays excluded after the first request is applied). Allowing a host takes it off the excluded list and the reverse. `placement.set` (whole lists, optional `expectedRevision`) stays in the state API. The proposal reason now says where local-only data may go is shown first.
- The test now proves the placement itself: with nothing listed the dispatcher's start on a host fails with the data-location reason and no host is offered the attempt; after the owner lists a host the next task starts there. A mutation that skips the policy in the service's placement check fails.
- Left: the enrolled-host listing pages by 200 (not exercised by a test); when the operator passes their own `placementPolicy`, `placement.get` shows the setting-based hosts, which that policy does not use.

## H02d: the remaining composed-controller proofs of remote stop, checkpoint fencing, routes and relocation refusals
- `api/testing/remote-world.ts` (new, shared with `start-remote-fencing.test.ts`): the composed controller with remote hosts, a movable clock and an agent with tasks; hosts can announce other capabilities and the requirements and checkpoint wait are options.
- `api/start-remote-proofs.test.ts`: (1) the owner's stop asks the worker for a last checkpoint through its own control poll, waits for the answer, ends the placement, records the checkpoint and the worker is fenced on poll, heartbeat and result and is offered nothing; an emergency stop does not wait; a host principal cannot stop an attempt. (2) A stop's checkpoint wait that is still open when the owner moves the attempt ends fenced and does not return the new host's checkpoint (the move is started first and the stop 1.5 s later, so its deadline is after the move; the margin only grows on a slow machine). The whole-text redaction before the limiter is belt and braces, since the limiter redacts too. ## H07e: the dispatcher passes over a host that would refuse the attempt (split from H07b)
- `WorkerHost.refuses(probe)` (optional) says why a host would refuse an attempt before a place is asked: `RemoteWorkerHost` asks `RemoteWorkerService.refusals` (what the host announced, its connection and the placement policy, the same rules `place` applies at the start). `#pickHost` skips such a host with its reasons and takes the next eligible one; before, the first fresh host was chosen and the attempt failed at the start when it refused.
- When every host refuses, the attempt waits (nothing is placed; the plan's `skipped` entry carries every host's reasons) and after `pinnedStaleTicks` (5) ticks a `dispatch_blocked` blocker tells the owner that no host will take it. A change of the setting (H07c) or a new host lets it start on the next tick. Hosts that are merely stale or revoked are still only a skip, as before.
- `requirements(order)` is asked of a preview order without a credential, since the real order does not exist yet; an operator function that reads the credential gets an empty one.
- Test: `api/start-remote-choice.test.ts` (r1 first in the order but unlisted: r2 gets it, r1 offered nothing; nobody listed: skip with both reasons, no failure, blocker after the threshold; owner lists r1: it starts there). Mutations: hosts not asked, blocker threshold never reached.
- Still H07b: the worker process runs the host poller; a poll ends when its client disconnects; the policy is checked again at delivery; the platform index drops revoked hosts and is filled at a restart.
- H07e review fixes: a host's answer says whether its reasons last (policy, what the host can do) or pass (not connected, not heard from lately, not yet announced); only lasting refusals by every candidate count toward the owner blocker, so a restart or a network drop never opens one. A host that cannot be asked (`refuses` throws) is tried and the placement judges it, with the fault going to `onError`. The refused-ticks counter is its own, consecutive and cleared on a plain skip or a start. Known: a mix of stale and refusing hosts stays a plain skip; each tick asks every candidate host per waiting attempt; the blocker's identity follows its text, as the pinned-host blocker's does.
- H07e re-review: the earlier composed test never reached `refuses()` while waiting (freshness skipped the host first), so the fixes are now proven in `dispatch/dispatcher.test.ts` with hosts that answer: passing reasons only skip; lasting ones by every host block at the third consecutive tick; a plain skip restarts the count; a throwing `refuses` is tried and reported to `onError`. Mutations (always count, throw counted, no reset) killed. Known: whether a reason lasts is read from its wording in `RemoteWorkerService.refusals` (a structured kind would be sturdier); a host missing the harness is a skip in `#pickHost` but lasting in `refusals`.

## Agent endings, submissions and integration (owner decisions 2026-10-28; Opus-reviewed design, no code yet)
- The agent ends its work with `work.end {submit, result, note, message}` ("submit and end" or "end"); the name avoids the controller command `attempt.finish` and Pi's `submit`. The controller completes the ending, so the agent's own call never waits on itself (H12n). A killed write call turns submit into end with a `release_failed` blocker.
- Before submitting, the author pulls the latest landing-branch head into its checkout with `work.refresh` (H12p), resolves its own conflicts and re-runs its checks; a submit on a stale base with overlapping files is refused with the head commit and the files. A per-project cap on refresh rounds (default 3) is followed by a reserved landing slot, then the director or owner.
- One active integrator per project (per landing branch), under a fenced expiring lease (P10); integrators are a pool across projects with fresh credentials and context each (P10b). The integrator re-applies mechanically and never writes content; a conflict goes back to the author.
- Landing is a per-project setting (P08, chat in P08b): `integration-branch`, `main-automatic` (must be possible in every profile when the owner sets it; no human step per landing) or `human-promotes`; installation default for new projects; strict defaults to a human, derived and autonomous to the integration branch; precedence installation lock > project > installation default > profile; the effective mode is saved at creation so a profile switch changes no project. `main-automatic` is an owner-only decision, audited, backed by an exact branch-scoped grant held only by the landing service (P10c); the controller derives protected branches itself (A07f), because today an agent's own `branchProtected` flag decides.
- Roles: `director` (the owner may label it "CTO") is separate from the supervisor link; author, reviewer, integrator, qa, docs; labels are display only (H11b). Submission kinds by role (Q01b). H12d is narrowed to the A06 release path and landing; H12l already wraps integration, refresh and quarantine.
